title: Kashmir
hook: a theater audience weeps at a tragedy and walks out into the night strangely at peace, and a Kashmiri teacher asks why

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kashmir, Kalhana's river of kings, told like a judge and meant to leave the reader calm.

On stage, a grieving lover cries out, and down in the seats people are wiping their eyes. Then the play ends, the lamps go out, and they walk home under the stars, talking quietly, somehow lighter than when they came. Nobody died in their house tonight. They wept anyway, and it did them good. Why does a sad story feel like a gift? A teacher in Kashmir thought hard about that question, and his answer reached all the way to Shiva. His name is Abhinavagupta.
screen: `TEARS IN THE THEATER.` → `LIGHTER ON THE WAY HOME.` → `ABHINAVAGUPTA ASKS WHY.`

segments.voice: Abhinavagupta is remembered as a teacher who wrote about two things that might seem far apart: the art of theater and poetry, and the way to Shiva. In his tradition they turn out to be close. Start with the theater. Indian poetics speaks of rasa, the taste of a work of art. In a tragedy there's real sorrow in the story, but it isn't your private sorrow. You don't have to fix anything or protect anyone. So the feeling comes to you loosened from your own small worries, and you can savor it, the way you savor a flavor. That's rasa. In that moment, Abhinavagupta explained, the viewer's little self, my problems, my plans, steps aside, and what's left is a kind of open, tasting awareness, with a quality of rest and wonder. Then he made the bold link. If a play can briefly lift us into wide, delighted awareness, that awareness isn't something the play adds. It was there all along. And in his Shaiva teaching, that wide awareness is what Shiva is. The theater gives a glimpse, borrowed, for an evening. The path is about seeing it without the borrowing. Tradition adds an ending to his own story: one day he walked into a cave with his disciples, chanting, and was not seen again. Kalhana's river flowed toward calm. Abhinavagupta's road runs through a theater, to the same quiet.
screen: `THEATER AND SHIVA, TOGETHER` · `RASA: THE TASTE OF ART` · `THE SMALL SELF STEPS ASIDE` · `THE AWARENESS WAS ALWAYS THERE`

segments.voice: Let a little of the feeling from a song, a film or a story that once moved you return. Then gently notice what's noticing it: the feeling comes and goes, but something is aware of it the whole time, wide and quiet. Rest there, in the tasting, without needing the feeling to stay.
Kashmir. The valley where Abhinavagupta taught that the taste of a play, the rasa, is a glimpse of the wide awareness his tradition calls Shiva. Today's word.
Your line: Kashmir. On this view, the quiet behind every play was there all along. Day one thousand three hundred ninety, done.

howItsDone: Students of Kashmir Shaivism and of Indian poetics read Abhinavagupta's writings with teachers, and his account of rasa is still taught to students of classical dance, music and theater.

chat.meaning: For Abhinavagupta, rasa comes when the little self steps aside; that open, tasting awareness is, in his Shaiva teaching, Shiva.
